newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: BellSouth/Clear concerned at spectrum auction plan.
newsitem.headline: BellSouth/Clear concerned at spectrum auction plan.

text.p: BellSouth and Clear Communications are unhappy with the Commerce Ministry's draft plans for management for next year's spectrum auction, Infotech Weekly reported on Monday.
The plans were made public by the Commerce Ministry two weeks ago in a run-up to a planned multi-million dollar spectrum auction next year, expected to attract many bidders.
Craig Holmes, Clear Communications strategic development directory, told InfoTech Weekly that Clear was not happy about the potential for anti-competitive capture of spectrum.
The ministry was relying on the anti-competitive measures of the Commerce Act, which he said Clear had little faith in. Clear would prefer a more interventionist approach, he said.

The draft report deals with the two-gigahertz band which, although already used by TVNZ for programme transmission and Trans Power to monitor the national power grid, can be used for new personal communications services. These services represent a critical future market and range from complex cellular-like services such as wireless PABX to cordless phones used in the home. It uses a range of standards.
The report proposes creation of 32 management rights within the band.
Clear and BellSouth are concerned the open auction process will enable Telecom, through its financial clout, to dominate.

Holmes said a player may buy spectrum and then not use it as a means to exclude entrants. A "use it or lose it" approach needed to be taken with the spectrum going to the next highest bidder, he said.
BellSouth said the report had not addressed competition issues associated with the allocation of spectrum.

"BellSouth believes that no further spectrum allocations, required to support cordless services, should be made until such time as a full assessment of competition issues has been made and adequate competition safeguards are implemented."
BellSouth wants further consideration of the issue before the release of spectrum.

Allan Collins, Telstra national manager for network technology, said incumbents might be in trouble as they would either have to rebid for spectrum or eventually move. While there were sunset clauses, he said issues for existing users might be complex.
Murray Milner, Telecom's general manager for network development, said the company supported an open market approach and was generally supportive of the draft plan.
"Telecom believes the market mechanism should be the grounds for allocation of spectrum."
